2.text: I must mention also a special performance of the walrus-hunt, which is

3.text: performed without preparation, and generally on the last day of the great

4.text: winter ceremonial. In this the men and the women sit down opposite each

5.text: other, in two rows, and beat their palms, exclaiming, “Ha, ha, ha!” The men,

6.text: from time to time, swing their arms, as if brandishing an imaginary spear.

7.text: I had no opportunity to witness a performance of this kind, which is

8.text: considered by the people as having the character of a play or a dance.

9.text: Among the Kamchadal, not more than forty years ago, there were observed

10.text: various performances of a similar character, in which the hunting of the whale,

11.text: the wolf, and the bear, was represented. Krasheninnikoff mentions such per-

12.text: formances in even earlier times. He had the good-fortune to witness them

13.text: in several villages. In modern times these performances have been thoroughly

14.text: Russianized, and blended with popular dramatic performances of the cossacks,

15.text: brought by them from Russia. I had an opportunity of witnessing a perform-

16.text: ance of such a kind in the village of Tighil. It represented a trip of cos-

17.text: sack pirates in a boat, and was almost devoid of local features.

18.text: Tossing on Walrus-Hide. — The “tossing on walrus-hide” forms among

19.text: the Maritime Chukchee, and especially among the Asiatic Eskimo, an extra

20.text: ceremonial (Plate XXXIII, Fig. 3), which is arranged in early or middle summer

21.text: in order to ward off danger from contagious diseases or to assuage too long

22.text: and violent tempests. The “tossing on the walrus-hide” is considered akin

23.text: to the races, and the family who arrange the ceremonial are called simply

25.text: On the day chosen for the ceremonial, numerous guests gather at the

26.text: house of the “racers.” The women of the family bring sacrifices to “all the

27.text: directions.” Then a feast follows, at the end of which the house-master, or still

28.text: better a shaman from among his nearest relatives, if there be any such, paints

29.text: with red ochre the faces of all those who have recently been taken ill; also

30.text: those who look sickly, and concerning whom there might be apprehension of

31.text: an attack by keˊlet. Small children, with hardly an exception, are painted.

32.text: The marks of the painting are varied, and closely resemble those of the

33.text: painting with reindeer-blood in the “slaughtering-ceremonials” of the Reindeer

34.text: Chukchee. After that, the tossing begins. Men and women seize a big

35.text: walrus-hide (split in two to make it thinner), grasping it firmly by loops cut

36.text: around its outer edge, and lift it from the ground. Then the young men

37.text: and girls, one by one, or in pairs consisting of a man and a woman, try

38.text: their skill. For this, the performer plants himself firmly in the middle of

39.text: the hide, and with a sudden jerk those who hold it send him upward, often

40.text: to the height of five metres. After that involuntary jump, he falls back on

41.text: the skin, and is safe from harm. The greatest skill is in coming down on

42.text: the feet without losing one’s equilibrium. Women are more clever than men

43.text: at this, and there are those who can keep upright for three successive jumps.
